data.title: Tuberous sclerosis complex — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Tuberous sclerosis complex** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. Define tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC).**
- Autosomal dominant multisystem disorder (1 in 6000) with hamartomas in skin, brain, kidneys, heart, lungs and eyes, due to mutations in TSC1 (hamartin, 9q34) or TSC2 (tuberin, 16p13 — more severe) → loss of inhibition of mTORC1 (mammalian target of rapamycin) → cell growth; ~2/3 de novo
- Classic Vogt triad: seizures, intellectual disability, facial angiofibromas (epiloia) — present in <50%

**Q2. Describe the clinical features, criteria and diagnosis (PYQ) — 2021 criteria.**
- Major (11): hypomelanotic macules (≥3, ≥5 mm), angiofibromas (≥3) or fibrous cephalic plaque, ungual fibromas (≥2), shagreen patch, multiple retinal hamartomas, multiple cortical tubers and/or radial migration lines, subependymal nodules (≥2), subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA), cardiac rhabdomyoma, lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), angiomyolipomas (≥2)
- Minor (5): 'confetti' skin lesions, dental enamel pits (>3), intraoral fibromas (≥2), retinal achromic patch, multiple renal cysts, non-renal hamartomas, sclerotic bone lesions
- Definite TSC: 2 major or 1 major + ≥2 minor features, or identification of a pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variant; possible: 1 major or ≥2 minor (LAM + angiomyolipomas alone = need another feature)

**Q3. Write a short note on adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas) (PYQ).**
- Misnomer — they are angiofibromas (not sebaceous adenomas): symmetrical, smooth, red-pink, dome-shaped papules on nasolabial folds, cheeks and chin (sparing upper lip), appearing at 2–5 years and increasing at puberty; ~75–90% of TSC
- Histology: dermal fibrosis with stellate fibroblasts, dilated capillaries, absent elastic tissue, atrophic follicles
- Treatment: topical sirolimus (rapamycin 0.1–1%) — first line; PDL, CO2/Er:YAG laser ablation, shave excision, electrosurgery

**Q4. Write a short note on the shagreen patch (PYQ).**
- Connective tissue naevus (collagenoma): irregular, slightly elevated, skin-coloured to yellowish-brown plaque with orange-peel ('pig-skin'/shagreen leather) surface, usually on the lumbosacral area; appears in early childhood (~50% of TSC)
- Histology: thickened, densely packed collagen bundles in dermis

**Q5. Other skin signs.**
- Hypomelanotic macules (earliest sign — at birth; ash-leaf shape, polygonal 'thumbprint', confetti macules on limbs; best seen with Wood's lamp; poliosis)
- Fibrous cephalic plaque (forehead — yellowish-brown plaque, often first facial sign)
- Ungual fibromas (Koenen's tumours — periungual/subungual flesh-coloured papules after puberty, toenails > fingernails; longitudinal groove in nail)
- Intraoral (gingival) fibromas, dental enamel pits, molluscum pendulum, café-au-lait macules (not specific)

**Q6. Systemic manifestations.**
- CNS: cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, SEGA (obstructive hydrocephalus), seizures (infantile spasms — West syndrome), intellectual disability, autism, TAND (TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders)
- Kidney: angiomyolipomas (bleeding — leading cause of death in adults), cysts (TSC2/PKD1 contiguous gene syndrome), renal cell carcinoma
- Heart: rhabdomyomas (fetal/neonatal — regress), arrhythmias (WPW)
- Lungs: lymphangioleiomyomatosis (women — pneumothorax, chylothorax), multifocal micronodular pneumocyte hyperplasia
- Eyes: retinal hamartomas ('mulberry'), achromic patches

**Q7. Investigations and surveillance.**
- MRI brain (every 1–3 years until 25 y — SEGA), EEG, renal MRI (every 1–3 years), echocardiography and ECG (infancy), HRCT chest (women ≥18 y), ophthalmology, dental exam, neuropsychiatric assessment; genetic testing; examine parents

**Q8. Management.**
- mTOR inhibitors: everolimus (SEGA, angiomyolipomas, refractory seizures), sirolimus (LAM; topical for angiofibromas)
- Vigabatrin for infantile spasms; other antiepileptics; epilepsy surgery
- Embolisation/nephron-sparing surgery for bleeding angiomyolipomas
- Skin: topical sirolimus, lasers, excision of ungual fibromas and shagreen patches if symptomatic
- Genetic counselling (50% risk; germline mosaicism in apparently unaffected parents)

**Q9. Classify multiple tumour syndromes (PYQ).**
- With adnexal tumours: Cowden (trichilemmomas, acral keratoses, oral papillomas — PTEN; breast/thyroid/endometrial cancer), Muir–Torre (sebaceous neoplasms + visceral cancers — mismatch repair), Brooke–Spiegler/familial cylindromatosis (CYLD — cylindromas, spiradenomas, trichoepitheliomas), Birt–Hogg–Dubé (fibrofolliculomas, renal tumours, pneumothorax — FLCN), Gorlin (BCCs), Rombo, Bazex–Dupré–Christol
- With fibrous/neural/vascular tumours: TSC, NF1/NF2, Gardner (epidermoid cysts, osteomas, desmoids, colonic polyps — APC), MEN 2B (mucosal neuromas), Carney complex, Reed syndrome (multiple cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas + renal cell carcinoma — fumarate hydratase), blue rubber bleb, Maffucci

## Quick spotter facts
- Facial angiofibromas + ash-leaf macules + shagreen patch + Koenen's tumours — tuberous sclerosis (mTOR)
- Topical sirolimus for angiofibromas; everolimus for SEGA/AML

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Tuberous sclerosis); 2021 International TSC Consensus diagnostic criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
